"Formally" means in a formal way — that is, following proper rules, official procedures, accepted conventions, or strict definitions. It describes how something is done: through the right channels, in the right manner, or with the right degree of seriousness and structure.

Its natural opposite is "informally" — casually, loosely, without following strict rules.
The word carries the same underlying idea in all its uses, but it shows up in a few different contexts. Understanding each one will give you complete mastery of the word.
1. Following proper rules, etiquette, or conventions

This is the most everyday use. When someone does something "formally," they are doing it in a correct, proper, or ceremonial way — the way the rules or customs say it should be done.

They were formally dressed for the wedding. (following dress conventions — not just wearing anything casual)

He formally introduced himself to the committee. (with proper, polished manners — not just saying "hey, I'm John")

The evening began formally, with everyone taking assigned seats. (structured, by-the-book, not casual)

Here, "formally" is essentially the opposite of "casually" or "loosely."
2. Officially — through proper channels or processes

This is a very important use, especially in legal, government, business, and institutional language. When something happens "formally," it happens through the recognized, official process — not just as a private understanding or a verbal agreement, but as a proper, documented, or declared act.

She was formally appointed as the new CEO.

(She didn't just start acting like a CEO — she was officially, properly appointed through the right process.)

He was formally charged with fraud.

(The legal system officially brought charges against him — it became a matter of official record.)

The two countries formally signed the peace agreement.

(They didn't just informally agree to stop fighting — they went through the official, recognized ceremony and process.)

The government formally declared a state of emergency.

(An official, recognized declaration was made — not just an internal discussion.)

The key idea here: something can exist informally (everyone knows it, everyone acts on it) but until it happens formally, it has no official standing. The boss may have been acting like the CEO for months, but she was only formally appointed on Tuesday.
3. In a strict, precise, or rigorous sense

This use is common in academic writing, mathematics, philosophy, and science. When a writer says "formally," they mean "according to strict, careful, rigorous definition" — not just loosely or in everyday terms.

Formally, a prime number is defined as a natural number greater than 1 with no divisors other than 1 and itself.

(This is the precise, technical definition — not a rough approximation.)

Formally speaking, these two concepts are distinct, even though people often use them interchangeably.

(In strict, careful usage, they are different — even if most people blur the line.)

The theory was never formally proven.

(It was never proven in a rigorous, accepted mathematical or scientific sense — there may be strong informal evidence, but not a formal proof.)

This use signals: I'm being careful and precise here, not loose or casual.
4. In terms of outward form — even when the reality is different

This is a subtler but very useful sense. Sometimes "formally" is used to describe the official or surface-level situation, even when the actual reality on the ground is quite different.

The two companies are formally separate, but they are owned by the same person and share all their resources.

(On paper — officially, legally — they appear to be two independent companies. In practice, they aren't really.)

He remained formally in charge, but had lost all real power.

(His title still said he was in charge. The official structure still put him at the top. But in reality, others were making every decision.)

The two countries were formally at peace, but there was constant tension on the border.

(There was no official declaration of war. But peace was barely real.)

This sense highlights a gap between what is officially true and what is actually true.

The single most important thing for learners: "Formally" vs. "Formerly"

These two words are very commonly confused because they look and sound similar. They mean completely different things.

  • Formally → in a formal/official/proper way (how something is done)
  • Formerly → previously, in the past (when something happened — no longer true now)

She was formerly the CEO. = She used to be CEO. She is no longer CEO now.

She was formally appointed as CEO. = She was officially, properly appointed as CEO (and presumably still is).

The city was formerly known as Bombay. = In the past, its name was Bombay. Now it's Mumbai.

The city was formally renamed Mumbai. = There was an official act that changed the name.

One simple way to remember: "formerly" contains the word "former" — as in "former president," meaning someone who used to be president but isn't anymore. If you're talking about the past, use "formerly." If you're talking about how something is done (officially, properly, by the rules), use "formally."
Quick summary of all the senses

"Formally" always means doing something according to the proper, correct, or official standard — whether that's:

  • Following rules of etiquette and convention (formal dress, formal behavior)
  • Going through official processes (formally appointed, formally charged)
  • Using rigorous, precise definitions (formally defined, formally proven)
  • Describing the official surface even when reality differs (formally separate, formally in charge)

The thread running through all of them is the same: structure, official recognition, proper procedure, or strict precision — as opposed to casual, unofficial, loose, or approximate.
